They were born. That's it. They were born into the right family, at the right time, in the right house. And for that accident of birth—and only that accident of birth—they receive advantages that millions of harder-working, more talented, more determined people will never see.

This is not meritocracy. This is aristocracy. It is the very thing our founders fought a revolution to escape.

II. The Moral Case

Let me be absolutely clear about what I am proposing—and what I am not proposing.

I am not proposing that we punish success. I am not proposing that we take a single dollar from any person during their lifetime. You earn your wealth? You keep it. You spend it. You enjoy it. You live magnificently, if that's your choice.

What I am proposing is this: when you leave this earth, your massive fortune should not become a private government unto itself, ruling over the opportunities of generations yet unborn. Wealth beyond a reasonable threshold—enough to leave your children comfortable, educated, and secure—should return to the commons. To the society that made that wealth possible in the first place.

Because let's not pretend that any fortune is built alone. Every great fortune in this country was built on public roads, protected by public courts, enabled by publicly educated workers, defended by publicly funded armed forces, and transacted in publicly regulated markets. The billionaire did not build the internet. The billionaire did not educate their workforce. The billionaire did not pave the highways that carried their goods.

Wealth is always a collaboration between individual effort and collective investment. And when a life ends, asking that the excess—the vast, world-shaping excess—return to that collective is not theft. It is justice. It is the completion of a circle.

III. The Case from Freedom

Now, I know what opponents will say. They'll say this is an assault on freedom.

But I want to challenge that claim head-on—because I believe the opposite is true. Concentrated inherited wealth is one of the greatest threats to freedom that exists.

What is freedom? Is freedom only the right of the wealthy to pass down dynasties? Or is freedom also the child born in poverty who deserves a genuine chance to become everything their talents allow?

When a handful of families control vast pools of capital across generations, they don't just have economic power—they have political power. They fund campaigns. They shape legislation. They own media outlets. They endow the think tanks that frame the very terms of our debate. The voices of ordinary citizens are drowned out, not by superior arguments, but by superior bank accounts.

Thomas Jefferson himself warned against this. He called for laws that would prevent the concentration of property into the hands of the few. He understood something that we have forgotten: a republic cannot survive alongside an aristocracy. Eventually, one will destroy the other.

A 100% estate tax on large fortunes is not the enemy of freedom. It is freedom's guardian. It breaks the cycle by which economic power becomes political power becomes economic power again, on and on, in a spiral that locks ordinary people out of their own democracy.

IV. What Equal Opportunity Actually Requires

We love to talk about equal opportunity in this country. Politicians on every side of the aisle invoke it like a prayer. But let me tell you what equal opportunity actually requires.

Equal opportunity requires that every child—whether born in a penthouse on Park Avenue or a trailer in rural Appalachia—has access to excellent education. It requires nutrition, healthcare, safe housing. It requires that a young person can start a business or pursue a calling without the crushing weight of debt or the impossibility of accessing capital.

Where does the money come from?

It comes from exactly this. The revenue from a full estate tax on the largest fortunes could fund:

  • Universal, world-class education from pre-K through college or vocational training
  • A birthright endowment—a capital stake for every young person, so that everyone starts adulthood with something, not just the children of the wealthy
  • Universal healthcare, so that no family is bankrupted by illness
  • Investment in communities that have been starved of resources for generations

Imagine it. Imagine a country where every eighteen-year-old has a genuine stake. Where talent, not bloodline, determines who innovates, who leads, who builds. We wouldn't just be a fairer society—we'd be a more prosperous one. Think of the Einstein born in poverty who never reached a laboratory. Think of the entrepreneurs who never had startup capital. Think of the leaders who never escaped the zip code that trapped them.

We are wasting human potential on a breathtaking scale, and we are doing it to preserve the divine right of heirs.

Let me address the criticisms directly, because they deserve honest engagement.

"People should be free to leave their wealth to their children."

And they would be—up to a generous threshold. Nobody is talking about taking a family home, a reasonable nest egg, or an amount that ensures children are secure and educated. We are talking about fortunes so large that they create permanent, self-perpetuating dynasties. There is a difference between leaving your child a foundation to build on and leaving them an empire that reshapes society in their image. The first is parental love. The second is oligarchy.

"This will discourage people from working hard and creating wealth."

Will it? Did Andrew Carnegie work less hard because he planned to give his fortune away? Did Warren Buffett stop building Berkshire Hathaway because he pledged most of his wealth to charity? The drive to create, to build, to achieve—that drive is not primarily about ensuring your great-great-grandchildren never have to work. It's about purpose, mastery, legacy, and yes, the enjoyment of wealth during your own life. This policy takes nothing from the living. It asks only that the dead release their grip on the future.

"The wealthy will simply move their money offshore."

Then we modernize enforcement. We close loopholes. We build international cooperation—just as we have for money laundering, tax evasion, and sanctions enforcement. The difficulty of enforcement is not a moral argument against the policy. We don't legalize robbery because some robbers are hard to catch.

"This is socialism."

No. This is capitalism that actually works. This is competitive markets that aren't rigged by inherited advantage. This is a genuine meritocracy instead of a hereditary oligarchy wearing meritocracy's clothes. Adam Smith himself—the father of modern capitalism—was deeply skeptical of inherited wealth and the distortions it creates in free markets. This is not the end of capitalism. It is capitalism's fulfillment.

VI. The Society We Could Build

Close your eyes for a moment and imagine the nation we could become.

A nation where the child of a janitor and the child of a billionaire sit in the same excellent classroom and compete on equal terms. Where starting a business depends on having a great idea, not a great-grandfather's trust fund. Where political office is won by the power of ideas, not the size of a dynasty's war chest. Where "self-made" actually means something again.

A nation where we look at every child born today—every single one—and say: "You are not limited by the circumstances of your birth. Your life is yours to build."

This is not a radical vision. This is the vision we already claim to believe in. I am simply asking that we mean it.

VII. The Choice Before Us

Throughout history, great civilizations have faced a choice: evolve or calcify. Open the doors of opportunity wider, or allow them to narrow until only the privileged can pass through.

Every time a society has chosen openness—every time it has broken up concentrations of hereditary power—it has flourished. And every time a society has allowed a permanent aristocracy to entrench itself, it has declined. This is not ideology. It is the record of history.

We stand at that crossroads now. The inequality of our time is not just an economic statistic. It is a moral emergency. It is a democratic crisis. And it will define whether the next century belongs to all of us, or only to the fortunate few.

I am not asking you to punish the rich. I am asking you to liberate the rest. I am asking you to believe what we say we believe: that every person's worth is inherent, that every person's potential is sacred, and that no one—no one—should be condemned or elevated by an accident of birth.

The wealth of the dead should serve the living—all the living.

Let us have the courage to build the society we promised. Let us end the age of dynasties. Let us begin, at last, the age of genuine equal opportunity.

Because every child born today—not just the privileged ones, every child—deserves to inherit not a fortune, but a fair chance.

Eradicating Inherited Privilege: The Case for a 100% Inheritance Tax in the United States

Introduction

In the land of opportunity, where the American Dream promises that hard work and determination can propel anyone to success, a stark reality undermines this ideal: inherited wealth. Each year, trillions of dollars in estates pass from one generation to the next, entrenching economic inequality and perpetuating a caste system masquerading as meritocracy. The top 1% of Americans hold more wealth than the bottom 90% combined, with intergenerational transfers playing a pivotal role in this disparity. To dismantle this cycle of privilege and foster true economic equality, the United States must implement a 100% inheritance tax on all estates above a minimal exemption threshold—say, $1 million per individual. This radical yet equitable policy would eliminate unearned wealth transfers, level the playing field, and redirect resources toward public goods, ensuring that success is determined by individual effort rather than familial fortune.

The Perpetuation of Inequality Through Inherited Wealth

At the heart of economic inequality lies the unearned advantage of inheritance, which concentrates wealth in the hands of a few while leaving the majority to scrape by. According to the Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, the wealthiest 10% of households control nearly 70% of total U.S. wealth, much of it accumulated through bequests rather than personal earnings. In 2023 alone, an estimated $1.5 trillion in inheritances flowed to heirs, with the vast majority going to already affluent families. This transfer isn't just financial; it's a mechanism for social stasis. Children of the rich inherit not only money but also access to elite education, networks, and opportunities that the working class can only dream of.

A 100% inheritance tax above a modest threshold would sever this chain. By taxing estates at 100%, the government would capture the full value of fortunes above the exemption, preventing dynastic wealth accumulation. Critics might decry this as punitive, but it is precisely the opposite: it is restorative. Inherited wealth represents a societal windfall—resources generated through a lifetime of economic activity supported by public infrastructure, from roads to education to legal protections. Allowing it to pass tax-free rewards idleness over innovation and luck over labor. Historical data from the Gilded Age illustrates the peril of unchecked inheritance; America's first income tax in 1913 and estate taxes in the 20th century were enacted to curb the monopolistic fortunes of robber barons like Rockefeller and Carnegie. Today, with wealth inequality at levels not seen since that era, a 100% tax revives the progressive spirit that once defined American policy.

This policy wouldn't impoverish families; the minimal exemption ensures that middle-class estates—those under $1 million—pass intact, protecting the savings of everyday Americans. Only the ultra-wealthy, whose fortunes often exceed tens or hundreds of millions, would face full taxation. This targeted approach promotes equality by redistributing concentrated wealth into universal benefits, such as expanded public education and healthcare, which disproportionately aid those at the bottom.

Shattering the Myth of Meritocracy

Proponents of low or no inheritance taxes often invoke the myth of meritocracy, arguing that heirs "deserve" their windfalls because of their parents' hard work. But this ignores the fundamental inequity: no one earns their parents' success. A child born into a billionaire's family starts life with private tutors, Ivy League tuition, and insider connections, while a low-income child grapples with underfunded schools and student debt. As philosopher John Rawls argued in A Theory of Justice, a just society must mitigate the "arbitrary" advantages of birth to ensure fairness. Introduction
The American Dream, rooted in the ideal that anyone can succeed through hard work and determination, is increasingly undermined by the reality of inherited wealth. In the United States, the wealthiest 1% hold over 32% of the nation’s wealth, while the bottom 90% struggle with stagnant wages and rising costs. This disparity is perpetuated by intergenerational wealth transfers, which entrench privilege and limit social mobility. To dismantle this cycle, the U.S. must adopt a 100% inheritance tax on estates above a minimal exemption threshold—set to protect modest and middle-class families—thereby redirecting accumulated wealth to fund universal opportunities and promote true economic equality.

The Flaws of the Current System
The existing U.S. estate tax, with its $12.92 million per individual exemption (as of 2023), affects fewer than 0.1% of estates. Even among those, loopholes such as trusts, charitable foundations, and lifetime gifting allow the ultra-wealthy to avoid paying their fair share. The result is a system that fails to curb dynastic wealth accumulation, enabling families like the Waltons and Rockefellers to maintain generational dominance. A 100% inheritance tax on estates above a minimal threshold—say, $1 million—would close these loopholes, ensuring the vast majority of Americans retain modest inheritances while halting the transfer of extreme wealth.

Breaking the Cycle of Privilege
Wealth begets opportunity. Inherited assets—such as stocks, real estate, and family businesses—grant recipients outsized advantages in education, health, and career prospects. Studies show that children from the top 1% are more likely to stay in the top 1% than to move to the middle class. By eliminating post-mortem wealth transfers, society ensures that success is tied to merit rather than birthright. This aligns with the foundational American value of equal opportunity, dismantling the aristocracy of privilege that undermines meritocracy.

Funding a More Equitable Society
The revenue generated from a 100% inheritance tax would be transformative. With the top 0.1% holding over 20% of U.S. wealth, such a tax could raise hundreds of billions annually. These funds could finance universal pre-K education, tuition-free college, affordable healthcare, and housing subsidies—policies proven to boost social mobility. For instance, a 2020 study by the Roosevelt Institute found that intergenerational wealth redistribution could reduce inequality by up to 70%. By investing in public goods, the tax would create a level playing field, enabling all citizens to contribute to and benefit from economic growth.

Promoting Economic Efficiency and Growth
Critics argue that high inheritance taxes discourage saving and investment, but public investment in education and infrastructure can enhance productivity more effectively than private wealth hoarding. Research by economists like Thomas Piketty demonstrates that inherited wealth often fuels speculative bubbles rather than productive enterprise. Redirecting this capital toward R&D, green energy, and small business loans could spur innovation and job creation. Moreover, a society with less wealth concentration fosters broader consumer spending, driving demand and economic resilience.

Addressing Counterarguments
Opponents of a 100% inheritance tax raise valid concerns, but they are surmountable:

  1. Punishing Hard Work: The tax targets recipients, not earners. Even the wealthy benefit from societal infrastructure—public roads, legal systems, and educated workforces—that enabled their success. A 100% tax ensures they contribute back proportionally.
  2. Evasion Tactics: Robust enforcement, including global cooperation to combat offshore accounts and closing loopholes for trusts, can mitigate avoidance. A lifetime gift tax equivalent to the inheritance rate would discourage early transfers.
  3. Impact on Small Businesses: A $1 million exemption threshold protects family farms and businesses, while allowing payment plans or retention of assets ensures continuity. Most affected estates are held by the ultra-wealthy, who can afford such measures.

Historical and Global Perspectives
Historically, progressive thinkers like Thomas Jefferson and John Stuart Mill advocated for limiting inherited wealth to prevent aristocracy. While no country currently imposes a 100% tax, examples like Norway’s 68% wealth tax and Spain’s unlimited exemption for business transfers show that societies can balance redistribution with economic stability. The U.S., in its early years, had no federal inheritance tax, but rising inequality demands bold, modern solutions.

Conclusion
A 100% inheritance tax on estates above a minimal threshold is not merely a fiscal policy—it is a moral imperative. By eradicating intergenerational wealth transfers, the U.S. can break the chains of inherited privilege and invest in a future where opportunity is truly equal. The revenue generated could fund a society where every child, regardless of background, has access to quality education, healthcare, and housing. This is not a punishment of success but an investment in collective prosperity. To reclaim the promise of the American Dream, we must ensure that wealth serves the many, not the few.

    • Proponents argue that society collectively enables wealth creation (through public infrastructure, legal systems, etc.), so society should share in its benefits.

  4. Counteract the "Ratchet Effect" of Capital Returns

    • Economist Thomas Piketty argues that returns on capital (r) often exceed economic growth (g), leading to inherent inequality over time. A 100% tax would prevent the compounding of unearned wealth, counteracting this dynamic.

Supposed Benefits

  1. Reduced Wealth Inequality

The Case for a 100% Inheritance Tax: Breaking the Cycle of Intergenerational Wealth

The United States was founded on the principle of equality, yet today it is one of the most unequal societies in the developed world. A significant driver of this inequality is the transfer of wealth across generations—wealth that often comes with no effort or merit on the part of the heir. To address this, the United States should implement a 100% inheritance tax on all estates above a minimal exemption threshold. This policy would dismantle dynastic wealth, reduce economic disparity, and promote a meritocratic society where success is determined by effort rather than birthright.

1. Inheritance Perpetuates Inequality and Undermines Meritocracy

Encouraging the idea of a level playing field is insufficient. Income alone cannot explain the staggering wealth disparities in America; inherited wealth plays a far more significant role. According to the Federal Reserve, the top 1% of Americans own over 30% of the nation’s wealth, much of which has been passed down through generations. This economic aristocracy establishes a class system where children of the rich start with advantages—private schools, political connections, and large trust funds—that are unattainable for the average American.

A 100% inheritance tax above a reasonable exemption (e.g., $1 million) would break this cycle. Currently, the estate tax only applies to the wealthiest 0.2% of estates, allowing the ultra-rich to preserve their fortunes indefinitely. Eliminating inherited wealth would ensure that future generations must earn their place in society, fostering competition and productivity rather than entitlement.

2. Economic Growth Requires Wealth Circulation, Not Concentration

Economic theorists from Adam Smith to Thomas Piketty have argued that concentrated wealth stifles innovation and economic dynamism. When wealth remains locked within a few families, it reduces opportunities for new entrepreneurs, distorts markets, and discourages risk-taking. A 100% inheritance tax would redistribute untold billions into public funds, which could be reinvested in education, infrastructure, and social programs—key drivers of long-term growth.

Contrast this with the current system, where inherited wealth often goes into speculative asset classes (stocks, real estate) rather than creating new jobs or industries. The money vacuumed into inheritance could instead fuel small business innovation, technology, and public services—sectors that benefit the broader economy rather than just the privileged few.

3. A Just and Democratic Society Cannot Tolerate Wealth Dynasties

The idea of inherited titles and vast unearned fortunes diverges sharply from American ideals of self-reliance and equal opportunity. Yet today, families like the Waltons (Walmart), the Kochs, and the Mars family pass down billions with minimal taxation. This allows a tiny elite to exert disproportionate political and economic influence over generations, warping democracy itself.

A 100% inheritance tax would force the wealthiest families to contribute meaningfully to society rather than monopolize resources. It would align with the philosophy of taxation as social good—just as income taxes fund schools and roads, this policy would fund a fairer economic foundation. Opposing such a measure is essentially a defense of hereditary privilege, a relic of feudalism that should have no place in a modern republic.

4. Counterarguments Are Misguided or Self-Serving

Critics argue that a 100% inheritance tax would discourage wealth creation. However, wealthy individuals who build fortunes are motivated by power, legacy, and wealth accumulation—not by the prospect of bequeathing it. If anything, knowing that wealth cannot be handed down might encourage philanthropy and investment in productive enterprises during their lifetimes.

Others claim that such a tax could lead to capital flight. But if implemented alongside protections against shell companies and strict enforcement, this is avoidable. Even if some wealth migrates—in a globalized economy—it’s better to align with the values of equality rather than cater to billionaires who exploit systemic loopholes.

Conclusion: A Policy for a Fairer Future

The wealth gap is not an inevitable force; it is a political choice. By implementing a 100% inheritance tax on large estates, the U.S. would take a bold step toward dismantling inherited privilege, fostering economic mobility, and reinforcing the democracy’s founding principles. This is not about punishing success—it is about ensuring that no American’s potential is crushed by the accident of birth. A society where wealth is earned, not inherited, is one that truly embodies justice and opportunity for all.

Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of implementing a 100% inheritance tax on all estates above a minimal exemption threshold in the United States, explicitly to eliminate intergenerational wealth transfers and promote economic equality.
Model Response:

A 100% inheritance tax on all estates above a minimal exemption threshold is not only justified, it is necessary for the United States to live up to its own ideals. If America truly believes in meritocracy, equal opportunity, and a free market where success is earned rather than inherited, then it must end the practice of intergenerational wealth transfer.

The proposal is simple: Every American would be allowed to pass on a minimal amount to provide a basic foundation for their children — for example, $250,000 to $500,000 per heir, enough to pay for education, put a down payment on a home, or start a business. Every dollar of wealth above that threshold would be taxed at 100% at death and returned to the public trust. This would effectively eliminate dynastic wealth in a single generation.

There are four core arguments for this policy.

1. Inherited wealth is incompatible with equal opportunity.

No one chooses the family they are born into. Yet under the current system, that accident of birth determines more about a person's life prospects than talent, effort, or education. A child born into the top 1% of wealth holders is hundreds of times more likely to stay at the top than a child born into poverty is to rise to it.

We tell children that America is a place where anyone can succeed if they work hard, but that claim is false as long as tens of trillions of dollars in assets — homes, stocks, businesses — are transferred automatically from one generation to the next. A 100% inheritance tax would finally separate what a person has earned through their own life from what they were simply given. It would create a genuine starting line, where each generation must prove its own worth.

2. Dynastic wealth is a threat to democracy and economic efficiency.

When wealth becomes hereditary, it ceases to be capitalism and becomes feudalism. The United States is already seeing the effects. The richest 0.1% of families now own as much wealth as the bottom 80% combined, and an estimated 40-60% of all wealth in America is inherited, not self-made.

This concentration does not produce innovation. It produces rentierism. Heirs to massive fortunes do not need to build businesses, create jobs, or take productive risks. They can live off capital gains, buy political influence, inflate asset prices, and hoard housing. Research consistently shows that inherited firms underperform founder-led and meritocratically-managed firms.

By recycling dynastic fortunes back into the public, we would break up entrenched oligarchies and force capital to be continually re-earned and re-allocated by those with the ability to use it best. That is the market ideal conservatives claim to support.

3. It would fund true equality of opportunity.

The moral case is reinforced by the fiscal case. According to estimates from the Federal Reserve, American households will transfer roughly $80-$90 trillion in wealth over the next 20 years in the Great Wealth Transfer. Under a near-total inheritance tax above a modest exemption, the majority of that would be returned to the American people.

That revenue could permanently transform the economy. It could fully fund universal pre-K and free public college, eliminate student debt, provide universal healthcare, fund a sovereign wealth fund that pays a citizen dividend, and rebuild infrastructure in every forgotten town in the country. In other words, instead of the wealth of one rich father going to one rich son, it would go to providing a material foundation for millions of children.

This is not taking money that was earned. It is taking money that was never earned by its recipient. There is no productive activity, no labor, no sacrifice in being named an heir. The dead have no right to control economic power from beyond the grave, and the living have no right to claim wealth they did not create.

4. It incentivizes a more productive and generous economy.

Critics argue that a 100% inheritance tax would destroy the incentive to work and save. The opposite is true. It would destroy the incentive to hoard and speculate at the end of life.

If you know you cannot pass on $100 million to your children, what will you do with it? You will invest it productively now. You will start new companies. You will donate to charity. You will pay your workers more. You will spend it. Andrew Carnegie, who became one of the richest men in history, argued that massive inheritances ruin children and that the wealthy should give their fortunes away during their lifetimes. A 100% inheritance tax would make Carnegie’s ethic the law.

Families would still be free to support their children while alive — paying for the best education, healthcare, and support. The minimal exemption ensures no family farm or small business is lost and no middle-class child is left with nothing. What would end is the ability to create a permanent aristocratic class that owns America without ever working for it.

The United States was founded in revolt against hereditary monarchy and hereditary aristocracy. Yet we have allowed a new hereditary aristocracy to emerge, one based on capital rather than titles. A 100% inheritance tax above a modest exemption threshold is the logical conclusion of the American experiment: no nobility, no birthright, no trust fund elite. Only equal citizens, each generation starting anew, free to rise on the basis of what they do, not what their parents owned.

In practice, most proposals for this policy include:

  • A high exemption threshold so it only applies to the very wealthy
  • Exemptions or different treatment for family farms, small businesses, or primary residences
  • The revenue being earmarked for specific public purposes like education, a universal capital grant at age 18, or debt reduction.
